question.text: Let $\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2\}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ If $\mathbf{b}_1=2\mathbf{c}_1-7\mathbf{c}_2$ and $\mathbf{b}_2=4\mathbf{c}_2-3\mathbf{c}_1,$ find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$
question.explanation:
The coordinates of the vectors in $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ are

\[ [\mathbf{b}_1]_{\mathcal{C}}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -7 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad [\mathbf{b}_2]_{\mathcal{C}}=\begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

Therefore, we obtain

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -7 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Let $\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2,\mathbf{b}_3\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2,\mathbf{c}_3\}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^3.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if

\begin{align*} \mathbf{b}_1&=\mathbf{c}_1+2\mathbf{c}_2-\mathbf{c}_3, \\[3pt] \mathbf{b}_2&=5\mathbf{c}_3+2\mathbf{c}_2, \\[3pt] \mathbf{b}_3&=\mathbf{c}_2-\mathbf{c}_1, \end{align*}

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to \mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{a} & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{b} & 1 \\ -1 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{c} & 0 \end{bmatrix}? \]
question.explanation:
The coordinates of the vectors in $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ are

\[ [\mathbf{b}_1]_{\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad [\mathbf{b}_2]_{\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad [\mathbf{b}_3]_{\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

Therefore, we obtain

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to \mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{2} & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{2} & 1 \\ -1 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{5} & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, $a=2,$ $b=2,$ and $c=5.$

question.text: Let $\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and let $\mathcal{S}$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}$ from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ if \[ \mathbf{b}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}_2=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\- 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
Recall that the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consists of the vectors $\mathbf e_1$ and $\mathbf e_2,$ given by \[ \mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The components of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

\[ [\mathbf{b}_1]_{\mathcal{S}}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad [\mathbf{b}_2]_{\mathcal{S}}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{S}.$

Therefore, we obtain \[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix

question.text: The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $\mathcal{C}$ to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ is given by $ P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 9 \\ -3 & -7 \end{bmatrix}. $ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ .
question.explanation:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}$, we get

\begin{align*} P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 9 \\ -3 & -7 \end{bmatrix}^{-1}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4 \cdot (-7) - 9 \cdot (-3)} \begin{bmatrix} -7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= (-1)\cdot \begin{bmatrix} -7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] & = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 9 \\ -3 & -4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text: The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $\mathcal{B}$ to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ is given by $ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}. $, Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ .
question.explanation:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$, we get

\begin{align*} P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}^{-1}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\cdot 5-(-3)\cdot (-3)} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 1\cdot \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] & = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text: The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $\mathcal{C}$ to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ is given by $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. $ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$
question.explanation:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}$, we get \begin{align*} P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4 \cdot (-1) - (-2) \cdot 1} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \left(-\dfrac 12 \right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] & = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac 12 & -1 \\ \dfrac 12 & -2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $\mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathcal{S}$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{S}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{e}_1,\mathbf{e}_2 \}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consists of the vectors \[ \mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{S}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix \[ M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 & \mathbf{e}_1 & \mathbf{e}_2 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \end{array} \right]. \]

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: \begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= R_2+(-2)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 1 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= \left(-1\right)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1 \end{array} \right] & R_1 &:= R_1+\left(-1\right)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ Therefore, we have \[ P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix \[ M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 & \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \end{array} \right]. \]

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 & 2 & 3 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= R_2 +R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 5 & 5 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= (-1) R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -5 \end{array} \right] & R_1 &:= R_1+(-1)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 8 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -5 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we have \[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 7 \\ -5 & -5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

question.text: Let $\mathcal{B}=\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 11 \end{bmatrix} \right\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \right\}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{C}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{c}_1$ and $\mathbf{c}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix \[ M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 & \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \end{array} \right]. \]

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & 3 & 2 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= R_2 +(-5)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 2 \end{array} \right] & R_1 &:= R_1+(-2)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 2 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ Therefore, we have \[ P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -4 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

example.title: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases

question.text: Let $\mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and let $\mathcal{S}$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{S}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{e}_1,\mathbf{e}_2 \}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consists of the vectors \[ \mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{S}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix \[ M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 & \mathbf{e}_1 & \mathbf{e}_2 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \end{array} \right]. \]

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & -6 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= R_2+(-3)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 1 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= \dfrac{1}{3}R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \dfrac{1}{3} \end{array} \right] & R_1 &:= R_1+3R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \dfrac{1}{3} \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ Therefore, we have \[ P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ -1 & \dfrac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix} \]

example.title: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases

question.text: Let $\mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\bigg\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix \[ M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 & \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \end{array} \right]. \]

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 9 & 6 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= R_2 +(-3)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & -12 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= -\dfrac{1}{3} R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \end{array} \right] & R_1 &:= R_1 +(-2)R_2\\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we have \[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \]
